group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 71-year-old man who resides on the long-term care wing of a suburban skilled nursing facility was transported to the emergency department late this morning after staff noted that his usual morning ambulation down the hallway left him more winded than normal and that he had developed a new, hacking cough productive of scant white sputum over the past twenty-four hours. According to the transfer paperwork, the patient’s baseline function involves wheelchair mobility for distances greater than fifty feet owing to residual right-hand clumsiness from a lacunar infarct five years earlier; he otherwise manages his own feeding and conversation without difficulty and is followed monthly by the facility’s speech therapist for mild dysarthria but has no cognitive impairment. There is no history of chronic kidney issues, dialysis, nephrolithiasis, or glomerulonephritis, and his outpatient metabolic panels have shown stable creatinine around 1 mg/dL; he similarly has never carried a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy, valve disease, or exertional orthopnea, and he denies prior episodes of lower-extremity swelling or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. His medication list includes low-dose aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine, sertraline for situational anxiety related to his placement in the facility, and a nightly senna tablet; he has never been prescribed loop or thiazide diuretics, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, or any cardiology device therapy. Nursing notes from the facility document an oral temperature no higher than 37.1 °C over the preceding week, but the patient had reported “feeling a little warm” and was given 650 mg of acetaminophen yesterday afternoon with minimal relief. He has completed the current season’s influenza vaccination and received both conjugate and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines two years prior. He quit cigarette smoking three decades ago after a 20-pack-year history, drinks no alcohol in the facility, and denies illicit drug use. There has been no recent travel outside the county, and no other residents on his hallway are currently on droplet precautions. On arrival he is seated upright on the stretcher, conversing smoothly with the triage nurse, oriented to name, location, date, and reason for visit, and able to recount his morning activities in detail, indicating intact mentation. Initial vital signs obtained before any therapeutic intervention reveal an oral temperature of 37.0 °C, heart rate 101 beats per minute in a regular rhythm, blood pressure 138/78 mm Hg measured manually, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute with relaxed diaphragmatic motion, and pulse oximetry 94 % on ambient air. Skin is warm, dry, and well perfused without diaphoresis or mottling; no jugular venous distention is visible at 30°. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a brisk S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, gallops, or extra sounds. Pulmonary examination reveals scattered late inspiratory crackles over the right posterior mid-lung zone with preserved breath sounds elsewhere; percussion is resonant throughout, and tactile fremitus is not increased. There is no accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, or pursed-lip breathing. The abdomen is soft and non-distended with normal bowel tones, and the liver edge is not palpable. Extremities are warm with brisk capillary refill, no pitting edema, and symmetric radial and dorsalis pedis pulses. Neurologic testing shows equal pupils, intact extraocular movements, normal facial symmetry, 5/5 strength in all limbs, and no new focal deficits compared with baseline. An arterial blood gas drawn on room air prior to any supplemental oxygen demonstrates pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, PaO₂ 85 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 22 mEq/L. Initial laboratory studies processed within twenty minutes of arrival reveal white blood cell count 11.0 × 10⁹/L with 78 % neutrophils, hematocrit 48 %, hemoglobin 16.0 g/dL, platelet count 210 × 10⁹/L, basic metabolic panel notable for sodium 146 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate matching the ABG, blood urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and a serum glucose of 102 mg/dL measured midday without recent food intake. High-sensitivity troponin is below detection threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any intravenous fluids or antibiotics shows a right upper-lobe airspace opacity with prominent air bronchograms but sharp costophrenic angles and no layering density suggestive of fluid; cardiac silhouette is within normal limits, mediastinum is unremarkable, and there is no cavitation or nodularity. Electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 100 beats per minute, PR and QRS intervals within reference range, and no ST-T changes. Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and comprehensive respiratory pathogen PCR panel were collected prior to therapy. At the time of this examination, the patient has received no antipyretics since arrival, no antibiotics, bronchodilators, diuretics, anticoagulants, vasoactive agents, or supplemental oxygen, and remains hemodynamically stable, maintaining his spontaneous respiratory effort with minimal distress while awaiting final disposition from the emergency physician.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using pretreatment findings.
- Demographics: a man's age in years gives 71 points; nursing-home residence adds 10.
- Comorbidities: prior lacunar stroke qualifies as cerebrovascular disease (+10). No documented malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, or renal disease (+0).
- Examination: mentation is normal, RR 17 is below 30, systolic BP 138 is at least 90, temperature 37.0°C is neither below 35 nor at least 40, and pulse 101 is below 125. Each scores 0.
- Tests: pH 7.35 is not below 7.35; BUN 17 is below 30 mg/dL; sodium 146 is not below 130 mEq/L; glucose 102 is below 250 mg/dL; hematocrit 48% is not below 30%; room-air PaO₂ 85 is not below 60 mm Hg. There is no pleural effusion. Each scores 0.
Sum: 71 + 10 + 10 = 91 (risk class IV).
Final answer: 91
